results.title: Your Roses Need These 6 Things Before the Ground Freezes
results.description:
📕 The Flower Gardener's Bible → https://bloomrelay.co/

Still deadheading your roses in autumn? This is the six-job sequence for getting roses ready for winter, set by the thermometer rather than the calendar. While the days are still mild: stop deadheading so the plant can set rose hips, stop feeding (no nitrogen this late), clean up every black spot leaf and diseased cane, and keep watering deeply right up until the ground freezes. After the first hard frost at 28 °F (about -2 °C), tidy the canes: hybrid teas and grandifloras down to about 3 feet, floribundas to 18-24 inches, just enough to stop wind rock, with the real pruning left for late winter. After the second hard freeze at 20 °F (about -7 °C), mound 6 to 8 inches of decomposed manure, topsoil or shredded bark over the base to protect the graft union, or use a rose cone. Then why the order matters so much, and why warmer winters make the thermometer the better guide. Whether you grow hybrid teas, floribundas, grandifloras or wild roses, this is what the botanical gardens and extension services actually say.

results.description:
Winterize roses before the first hard freeze with eight jobs in the right order, for a bed, a fence row, a climber, or a pot.

results.title: 🔥 УКРЫВАЮ НА ЗИМУ ТОЛЬКО ТАК! Как утеплить розы и гортензии
results.description:
Укрытие роз, гортензий, вейгел и голубики на зиму: какие материалы действительно спасают от мороза и выпревания, а какие только вредят. Спанбонд, лапник, торф, опилки, листва дуба и клёна — их эффективность и правила использования. Почему солома привлекает мышей, плёнка не дышит, а чёрный спанбонд перегревает. И как защитить укрытие от вредителей и болезней с помощью биопрепаратов.

🍂 Розы ещё радуют глаз в середине октября, но скоро придётся укрывать их на зиму. Вместе с ними вейгелы, крупнолистные гортензии и молодые посадки голубики. Чем лучше укрыть? Объединяя научные данные и личный опыт, могу сказать следующее.

🔥 Лучший материал: спанбонд или лутрасил.
Плотный белый нетканый материал с плотностью 60 г/м² и выше. Но есть нюанс: для хорошей работы нужен каркас. Подойдут палочки, ящики или металлические конструкции. Если поставить пластиковый ящик и сверху натянуть спанбонд, растения отлично перезимуют, защищённые от иссушающих морозов и перепадов температуры.

✅ Альтернативы:
Хвойный лапник. Эффективность около 80% от спанбонда, но не сохраняет тепло. В снежную зиму хорошо защищает от морозов. Лучше комбинировать: лапник сверху накрыть спанбондом без каркаса.
Окучивание грунтом. Даёт 75% эффективности. Минус: при затяжных дождях напитывается влагой, возможны выпревание и вымокание почек.
Верховой торф. Лёгкое антисептическое действие, защищает от выпревания. Намокает медленно. Идеально: торф, сверху лапник, затем спанбонд. Под таким укрытием перезимуют даже прихотливые гортензии.
Опилки. По научным данным 70%, но я сравниваю их со спанбондом. Они легко намокают и создают ледник весной. Зато в Беларуси это плюс: задерживает вегетацию и спасает от возвратных заморозков.
Опавшая листва. Быстро намокает, сгнивает и уплотняется, теряя свойства к февралю. Используйте листву дуба или клёна (содержат дубильные вещества) и обязательно накрывайте спанбондом.

⚠️ Что не использовать:
Солома. Главный магнит для мышевидных грызунов.
Полиэтиленовая плёнка. Не дышит, под ней всё запревает.
Чёрный спанбонд. Нагревается на солнце даже зимой, перепады температур слишком резкие.
Отцветшие стебли многолетников и летних цветов. Слабые утеплители, на них зимуют паутинный клещ и болезни.

✅ Защита от вредителей и болезней:
Перед укрытием посыпьте вокруг куста чайную ложку Квадросанита (от вредителей), чайную ложку Мышибало (отпугнёт грызунов) и чайную ложку Трихосана (защита от грибковых инфекций и выпревания). Тогда не придётся дополнительно опрыскивать растения. Они прекрасно перезимуют.

results.title: Winterizing Roses for Montana Winter | Northern USA, Canada, Northern Europe
results.description:
Winterizing Roses for a Montana Winter | Northern USA, Canada, Northern Europe | Zone 4b

If you grow roses in a cold winter climate — Northern USA, Canada, or Northern Europe — this video is for you.
We live in Northwest Montana, USA. That's -25°F to -20°F / -32°C to -29°C or lowere in winter. Same cold as many parts of North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Upstate New York, Maine, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, British Columbia Interior, and Northern Europe.
In spring I bought the Fragrant Rose Collection — Peak Performance (red), Oregold (yellow), Scentuous (pink), and Cl. Lavender Crush.
 Three are rated Zones 6-9, one is Zones 5-9. None are really rated for Zone 4b. I didn't know to check that when I bought them, and they were sold here like they were fine for this area. Now I have them, they grew all summer, and I want to keep them.

 In this video I show you my winterizing plan for a cold northern winter, step by step. This works for any cold climate where roses freeze, get windburn, or die back to the ground.

WHAT I'VE DONE SO FAR:
1. Individual hardware cloth tubes around each cane/bush
2. Soil mound 5-6 inches high piled around the cluster, covering the graft union
3. Tomato cages for support

My roses still have leaves right now, so I'm stopping here for now.

WHAT I'LL ADD AFTER THE LEAVES DROP:
 4. Straw mulch on top of the mound, pulled back from the canes
5. Burlap teepee, open at the top for ventilation
 6. Corn stalks outside as a windbreak

This is how I'm trying to get tender roses through a long, cold, windy northern winter.

If you're in the Northern USA, Canada, UK, Germany, Poland, Scandinavia, or anywhere with freezing winters, check the zone on the tag before you plant. Just because it's for sale in your area doesn't mean it's hardy for your winters.

 Where are you growing roses? Tell me your zone and country in the comments — USA, Canada, or Europe — and tell me what has worked for you to keep them alive.

Want more roses next June? What you do in October decides it. In this video, I share the 7 fall rose care steps that help your roses store energy, harden their wood, and set buds for far more blooms next year, including the one step most gardeners skip that protects the graft union through winter.

What state or USDA zone are you in, and when is your first hard frost?
Which of the 7 steps surprised you most?
I read every comment.

📌 QUICK REFERENCE

Stop deadheading about 6 weeks before your first frost
Use sulfate of potash in fall, not high-nitrogen fertilizer
Remove and bag black spot leaves, never compost them
Pull suckers from the root, never just cut them at ground level
Shorten tall canes by one third to prevent wind rock
Water deeply if the soil is dry 3 to 4 inches down
Add 2 to 3 inches of compost now, then mound the crown after your first hard freeze in colder zones

Always check product labels and your local extension office for advice specific to your region.

results.title: September Rose Care: 7 Jobs That Decide If Your Roses Survive Winter
results.description:
Your roses may look perfectly fine right now… but September is when you decide how they come through winter.

Some rose canes can already be dead while still looking green from the outside. The real damage often stays hidden until months later, when winter is over and there's nothing left to fix.

In this video, we're going through 7 important September rose care jobs designed around the problems that can quietly show up after winter.

🌹 Check your soil moisture and water deeply before the ground freezes so your roses aren't entering winter with a dry root system.

🌱 Stop the nitrogen. Late-season nitrogen can push soft new growth that may not have enough time to harden before frost.

🔎 Use the scratch test before pruning. A rose cane that looks healthy outside can be dead inside, while a rough-looking cane may still contain living green tissue.

✂️ Prune with restraint in fall. Remove dead and weak growth, reduce risky height where necessary, and save major structural pruning for spring.

🌿 Protect the graft union on grafted roses. That swollen point near the base can be one of the most vulnerable parts of the plant during a hard freeze.

🍂 Apply mulch at the right time and in the right way. The goal is winter root protection without keeping the plant too warm too early or creating a damp environment around the canes.

🧹 Clean up black spot, powdery mildew, spider-mite hiding places, and diseased debris. Leaving infected leaves and plant litter under the roses can carry problems straight into the next growing season.

The most important idea in this video is simple:

Don't wait for winter damage to tell you something went wrong.

September gives you a window to check what's happening below the surface, inside the canes, around the graft union, and under the rose bushes before those small problems become much bigger ones.

Your roses don't need to be pushed into more growth right now.

They need to be prepared for winter.

And the difference may not be obvious this month — it may only become obvious when spring arrives.

🌹 Before you leave your roses alone for winter, make sure you've done these 7 things.

Did you try the scratch test on your roses this year? What did you find — green tissue or more dead cane than you expected?

Tell me in the comments. 🌱

Many rose canes can appear green while hiding damage that only shows up after the frost. Proper rose care during September is crucial for successful winter preparation, ensuring your plants do not enter the cold season with weak roots or diseased foliage. 🌱

We are going through 7 essential jobs to protect your rose bushes. From using the scratch test to determine viability to managing mulch and rose pruning, these steps help you avoid common mistakes. results.description:
👉 Want to learn how to live a simpler, more independent life? Take a deeper look here: https://independentbackyard.com/my-book/#aff=natanaelfernamdes


Sixty-five degrees. That's the temperature where a Desert Rose's growth quietly shuts down, long before any frost warning ever reaches your phone. I am Elias Yoder, and today I'm giving you the exact winter protocol for Adenium obesum — and why treating it like any other cold-hardy succulent is exactly how so many of them are lost every year.

I farm in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. This plant has almost no margin for error around cold, even while it stays remarkably forgiving of nearly everything else. Today's video covers tracking overnight lows instead of daytime highs, deliberately choosing between a real winter rest or genuine active growth, cutting watering down to a fraction of summer levels, checking whether your plant is grafted, never risking an actual freeze, waiting until spring to prune cold damage, keeping even a dormant plant in real light, and reintroducing outdoor sun gradually in spring.
